ECE 6390

Code tracking and multipath bias

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows a direct code-correlation triangle with an in-phase echo 0.25 chip later at 0.3 of the direct voltage, and the early–late pair that balances 0.058 chip late.

Acquisition finds the code delay to within about a chip; tracking then keeps the local replica aligned as range and clocks change. A delay-lock loop correlates the received code with an early replica and a late replica separated by a spacing s in chips. When the prompt replica sits on the peak, the two side correlations are equal and their difference, the discriminator, is zero.

For an ideal wideband code the correlation is the triangle R(ε) = max(0, 1 − |ε|), with ε the replica delay error in chips. The discriminator D(ε) = |C(ε − s/2)| − |C(ε + s/2)| plotted against ε is the S-curve. It rises through zero at the lock point: a replica that is too late sees a larger early sample and is pulled earlier.

A reflected path adds a delayed copy: C(ε) = R(ε) + αe^(jφ)R(ε − δ), with relative amplitude α, excess delay δ in chips and carrier-phase difference φ. An in-phase echo raises the late side of the peak and pulls the lock later; an opposite-phase echo removes part of it and pulls the lock earlier. The direct arrival has not moved, so the measured range is biased.

For a short echo and s = 1 chip, the lock shifts by αδ/(1 + α) when φ = 0° and by −αδ/(1 − α) when φ = 180°. A narrower spacing samples the peak closer to its top and can reduce the bias. An echo delayed by more than 1 + s/2 chips no longer reaches either sample and leaves no bias.

Example

With α = 0.3 and δ = 0.25 chip, an in-phase echo moves the lock 0.3 × 0.25/1.3 = 0.0577 chip late, about 17 m at the 293 m GPS C/A chip length. The opposite-phase echo moves it 0.1071 chip early, about 31 m short. Narrowing the spacing to 0.2 chip reduces the in-phase bias to 0.030 chip.

Practice

1. Without any echo, where does the early–late discriminator balance, and why?

Use the symmetry of R(ε) = max(0, 1 − |ε|).

At ε = 0. The triangle is symmetric, so samples s/2 before and after the peak have equal correlation only when the prompt replica is exactly aligned.

2. Why can the same reflector produce opposite range errors at different times?

Follow the sign of αe^(jφ) as the carrier-phase difference changes.

The echo’s carrier phase depends on its extra path length in wavelengths. In phase, it adds to the late side and biases the range long; out of phase, it subtracts and biases it short. As the geometry changes, φ cycles and the error oscillates.
